title: Race, reading, & reporting
author: Alexander Russo
summary: Alexander Russo, who writes The Grade, argues that coverage of the renewed push for school integration in New York City needs more context and less assumption. He says last month's viral essay by Nikole Hannah-Jones revived the idea, and that he admires integration's vision but thinks it is unwise to pursue right now. He gathers voices from journalists, former chancellor David Banks and Hannah-Jones herself who question whether integration should outrank basic problems such as children who cannot read, absenteeism and under-enrolled schools. He proposes that reporters include where integration sits among real parent priorities, acknowledge that many scholars no longer treat it as a rigid priority, and recognise their own bias toward desegregation as the natural starting point. His view is that integration has not been durable and that the best way to improve it may be to improve school academics.
points: Russo argues that media coverage of integration should add context on real parent priorities, which rarely rank integration at the top.
Voices including former chancellor David Banks say a literacy crisis is a more fundamental problem than racial integration plans.
Reporters tend to presume desegregation is the universal starting point for fixing schools, a bias born of the Brown legend that deserves self-awareness.
Some scholars have moved away from treating integration as a rigid priority, and it was absent from a recent expert ranking of ideas for fixing schools.
His closing claim is that integration has not been durable and that improving school academics may be the best way to improve integration.
quotes: I admire the successes and the vision of school integration, but I believe it would be an unwise way to go right now.
I don’t have time to waste on efforts like that when I have a much more fundamental issue that’s sitting right in front of me, which is the fact that our kids can’t read
First and foremost, I propose that all articles on this topic include some information about where integration fits into real-life parent priorities.
Most parents agree that racial and economic integration is important and that they would like their children to attend schools with diverse enrollment
Last but not least, let’s acknowledge that there is a tendency among reporters to presume that deseg is the most important, universally admired option

Yes, in a perfect world, we could push for both integration and academics at the same time. But integration has not yet been as durable as it needs to be, and I fear spending more time and energy when the best way to improve integration may be to improve school academics.
